days.title: Little Places
days.verse: But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
body: Bethlehem wasn’t much to look at. Micah says it plainly — “little among the thousands of Judah.” A wide spot in the road. The kind of place folks pass through on their way to somewhere that matters.

We know a little about places like that. Hollers that don’t make the map. Towns where the post office closed, the school consolidated, and the young people moved off to Columbus. And yet God — “from of old, from everlasting” — had already picked out the little town. He wasn’t looking for impressive. He was looking for willing.

Today we light the first candle, the candle of hope. It’s a small flame in a big dark room. That’s the point. Hope rarely shows up in the capital city with a parade. It shows up small, in the places nobody’s watching — maybe even in yours.
days.prayer: Lord, thank You for seeing the little places. Start Your hope in mine. Amen.

days.title: Stumps Grow Kings
days.verse: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.
body: If you’ve ever cut a tree down to the stump, you know what happens come spring. Little green shoots push up out of what looked dead and done.

Jeremiah was preaching to a people whose kings had failed them. David’s family tree looked like a stump — proud once, then hacked down by bad choices and foreign armies. But God says, “the days come.” Not maybe. Not if things improve. They come. A righteous Branch will grow out of that stump, and He’ll do what every crooked king hadn’t: “execute judgment and justice in the earth.”

Some of us are staring at stumps this season. A marriage, a church, a body that doesn’t work like it used to, a family that’s seen hard years. Advent says God isn’t finished with stumps. He grows kings out of them.
days.prayer: Righteous Branch, grow something green in the places I’ve given up on. Amen.

days.title: Arise, Shine
days.verse: Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee.
body: December mornings come slow in the mountains. The sun has to climb over the ridge before it ever reaches the bottom of the holler, and some days it’s near ten o’clock before the frost on the creek bank lets go.

Isaiah says “Arise, shine” — but notice the order. First comes “thy light is come.” You aren’t asked to make light. You’re asked to stand up in it. The glory of the Lord rises on you the way the sun rises on a valley: whether the valley feels ready or not.

That takes some pressure off. Advent isn’t a contest to see who can glow the brightest. It’s an invitation to get up off the cold ground and turn your face toward what’s already coming over the ridge. Light has come. Your only job today is to rise and let it land on you.
days.prayer: Lord, I can’t make my own light. Rise on me, and I’ll stand up in it. Amen.

days.title: Good News for the Bound
days.verse: The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound.
body: Years later, Jesus would stand up in the synagogue at Nazareth, unroll this very scroll, read these very words, then sit down and say, “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.”

Look at who the good news is for: the meek, the brokenhearted, the captives, the ones in prison. Not the folks who have it all together. The ones who’ve been bound up — by addiction, by grief, by debt, by a past that won’t turn loose.

In these hills we’ve buried too many young people and watched too many families come apart. If that’s you, hear this: the Messiah didn’t come to scold the brokenhearted. He came to bind them up, the way you’d wrap a wound. He came to open the prison doors from the outside. Whatever has you bound this Advent, He was anointed for that.
days.prayer: Jesus, You came for the brokenhearted. Here’s mine. Bind it up. Amen.

days.title: More Than the Watchman
days.verse: I wait for the Lord, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.
body: Anybody who’s ever worked third shift knows what the psalmist means. Around four in the morning the hours go thick as molasses. You check the clock and it’s barely moved. You’re not wondering whether morning will come. You’re just waiting for it to get here.
That’s the waiting in this psalm. Not wishful thinking — watchman’s waiting. The sun has never once failed to come up, and the watchman knows it. His waiting is tired, but it is sure.

Advent teaches us to wait like that. Not “I hope things work out somehow,” but “in his word do I hope.” God’s promises are as dependable as daybreak. The night may be long — some nights are very long — but the watchman never waits in vain. Morning’s coming. Keep your post.
days.prayer: Lord, my soul is waiting. Hold me steady till morning. Amen.

days.title: Filled Up
days.verse: Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.
body: Mamaw never let anybody leave her kitchen hungry. You’d tell her you were full, and she’d put another biscuit on your plate anyway. “You’ll want it later.”

Paul prays a Mamaw kind of prayer here. He doesn’t ask that the Romans get a little hope, a polite spoonful. He asks the God of hope to fill them — “with all joy and peace” — till they “abound,” spill over, have more than they can hold.

And notice where it comes from: “in believing” and “through the power of the Holy Ghost.” This isn’t hope we work up by thinking positive. It’s served to us, heaped on the plate, by a God who is Himself the God of hope. If you’re running on empty this December, quit scraping the bottom of your own pot. Pull up a chair. He’s still filling plates.
days.prayer: God of hope, fill me up till it spills over onto somebody else. Amen.

days.title: Strength and Song
days.verse: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the Lord Jehovah is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
body: There’s a reason the old folks sang in the coal camps and around the kitchen table through the hard years. A song carries what a body can’t.

Isaiah says the Lord is “my strength and my song.” Strength gets you through the day. Song gets you through the night. God means to be both. And He doesn’t just hand you salvation and leave — He “is become” your salvation. He Himself is the thing that saves.

Notice too: “I will trust, and not be afraid.” Trust comes first; the fear leaving comes after. Most of us want it the other way around. But faith usually works like stepping onto a swinging bridge — you trust the cables before your knees quit shaking. As this week of hope ends, sing something today. Even if it’s quiet. Even if it’s shaky.
days.prayer: Lord, be my strength for the day and my song for the night. Amen.

days.title: Roadwork
days.verse: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
body: Anybody who drove the mountains before the four-lanes came through knows what a crooked road costs you. Switchbacks, washouts, a coal truck in front of you with nowhere to pass.

Isaiah pictures a road crew going out ahead of a coming King: fill the valleys, cut down the hills, straighten what’s crooked, so nothing slows Him down. John the Baptist took up these words and pointed them at our hearts. The road God wants smoothed doesn’t run through the desert. It runs right through us.

Today we light the second candle, the candle of peace. Peace often starts with roadwork. What’s in the way? A grudge you’ve been nursing. An apology you keep putting off. A habit you keep making excuses for. You don’t have to pave the whole thing today. Just roll one rock out of the road.
days.prayer: Lord, show me what’s in Your way in me, and help me move it. Amen.

days.title: Say It Twice
days.verse: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.
body: Some verses are long and full of thunder. This one’s short and soft, like a hand on your shoulder at the funeral home. “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.”
He says it twice. Folks who’ve sat with grief know why. The first time, you don’t hear it — the hurt’s too loud. Comfort has to come back around again, and maybe again after that.

These words came to a people in exile, far from home, who figured God had given up on them. And the first thing He says after all that silence isn’t “I told you so.” It’s comfort. “My people.” “Your God.” He’s still claiming them. If this season is heavier than it’s supposed to be — an empty chair at the table, a number you can’t bring yourself to delete from your phone — hear Him say it twice. You’re still His.
days.prayer: God of all comfort, say it again for me today. I need to hear it. Amen.

days.title: Suddenly
days.verse: Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the Lord of hosts.
body: Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament. After it, the prophets go quiet for about four hundred years. That’s a long time to hold onto a promise. Generations were born, grew old, and died waiting on “the Lord, whom ye seek.”

And then, Malachi says, He’ll come “suddenly.” Long waiting, sudden arrival — that’s often how God works. Like the first snow you’ve watched the sky for all week, and then you look up from the dishes and the whole yard’s gone white.

Malachi also says God would send a messenger first, to prepare the way. God doesn’t just drop in unannounced. He sends word ahead. He gets His people ready. Maybe you’ve been waiting a long time on something from God. Long silence doesn’t mean a broken promise. Keep your eyes on the window. Suddenly still happens.
days.prayer: Lord, keep me watching through the long quiet. Come suddenly. Amen.

days.title: Turning Hearts
days.verse: And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just; to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.
body: Of everything the angel could have said John the Baptist would do, look what’s near the top of the list: “to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children.”

Before the crowds, before the river, before “Behold the Lamb of God,” God’s preparation started at home. Families mended. Fathers who’d drifted turning back toward their kids. That’s what it looks like “to make ready a people prepared for the Lord.”

Christmas has a way of dragging every family’s cracks into the light. Somebody’s not speaking to somebody. Somebody didn’t get invited. Old hurts get warmed up right along with the leftovers. Peace on earth starts small — around one table, between two people. Whose heart needs yours turned back toward it? A phone call can travel a long way. So can a plate of fudge left on the porch, no note required.
days.prayer: Lord, turn my heart toward the ones I’ve drifted from. Start Your peace at my table. Amen.

days.title: Let Peace Make the Call
days.verse: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful.
body: The word Paul uses for “rule” is the word for an umpire — the one who makes the call. Let the peace of God be the umpire in your heart.
That’s worth chewing on. Most of us let something else make the calls. Worry makes them. Pride makes them. The news, the bank balance, and in December, the to-do list sure makes a lot of them.

Paul says peace gets the final word — and then he adds two things. “Ye are called in one body”: peace isn’t a solo sport; we keep it together. And “be ye thankful”: thankfulness is how peace keeps its job. It’s hard for worry to win an argument with a grateful heart. Before you decide anything big today, ask one plain question: does this come from peace? Then let peace make the call.
days.prayer: Prince of Peace, be the umpire of my heart today — and make me thankful. Amen.

days.title: Beautiful Feet
days.verse: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
body: Nobody ever called feet beautiful after a day of hauling hay or a double shift at the hospital. Feet are tired, blistered, dusty things.

But Isaiah does. “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings.” Picture a runner coming over the ridge with news from the battle while the whole town holds its breath. As he gets close they can see it on his face: we won. Peace. “Thy God reigneth!” Suddenly those muddy feet are the most beautiful thing in the world.

We know mountains. We know what it is to see somebody coming up the road and hope they’re bringing good news. This Advent, you get to be the runner. Somebody up your road is waiting on a kind word, a visit, a reminder that God still reigns. Your tired feet are beautiful when they carry that.
days.prayer: Lord, send my feet up somebody’s road today with good news. Amen.

days.title: The Dayspring
days.verse: Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.
body: Zacharias had been struck speechless for nine months. When his tongue finally came loose, this is what poured out: a song about the dayspring.
“Dayspring” is an old word for the first light of morning. Not the full sun — that first gray-gold seam along the top of the ridge, when the birds start up and you know the night is broken.

Zacharias sings that this light visits those who “sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.” Not walk. Sit. Some folks have stopped moving. They’ve sat down in the dark because they couldn’t see a way forward. And the dayspring doesn’t wait for them to get up and go find it. It visits. It comes to where they’re sitting. Then it guides — “our feet into the way of peace.” Light first, then a path. As this week of peace closes, let the light find you right where you sit.
days.prayer: Dayspring from on high, visit me where I’m sitting, and guide my feet. Amen.

days.title: Rejoice Anyhow
days.verse: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
body: Paul wrote this from a jail cell. Keep that in mind. He wasn’t on a porch swing with a full freezer and a paid-off truck. He was in chains, not sure whether he’d live or die, and he wrote, “Rejoice in the Lord alway.”
Then — maybe because he figured somebody would roll their eyes — he says it again: “and again I say, Rejoice.”

Mind the little words: “in the Lord.” Not rejoice in your circumstances. Not rejoice that everything’s fine. Paul’s joy drew from a deeper well than his situation, and that well never ran dry. Today we light the third candle — the rose-colored one, the candle of joy. It stands out on purpose. In the middle of the waiting, the church has always stopped to remember: joy isn’t a prize for when the waiting’s over. You’re allowed it right now, chains and all.
days.prayer: Lord, I’ll rejoice in You today — and if I forget, remind me again. Amen.

days.title: Magnify
days.verse: And Mary said, My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.
body: Mary was a teenage girl from a nowhere town, unmarried and expecting, with a story nobody was going to believe. If anybody had cause to worry what the neighbors would say, she did.

Instead, she sings. “My soul doth magnify the Lord.” To magnify something is to make it look bigger — like Papaw’s magnifying glass on the kitchen table, the one he used to read the seed catalog. Mary turns her whole life into that glass and holds it up so God looks bigger, not smaller, through her.

Here’s the thing about a magnifying glass: nobody looks at the glass. They look through it. Most of us spend a lot of energy trying to look bigger ourselves. Mary shows a better way. Hold your little life up to the light, and let folks see something bigger through it. That’s where the joy is.
days.prayer: Lord, make my life a magnifying glass. Let people see You bigger through me. Amen.

days.title: Dressed for the Wedding
days.verse: I will greatly rejoice in the Lord, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
body: There’s nothing like a mountain wedding — the bride coming down the aisle of a little white church, or across a field with the hills behind her, somebody’s aunt crying in the second pew.

Isaiah reaches for that picture. “He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness.” Notice: He hath clothed me. I didn’t sew it. I didn’t buy it. I showed up in my work clothes, and God dressed me for the wedding.

That’s the gospel in one verse. We don’t earn our way into God’s joy by getting cleaned up first. He does the clothing. He covers what we couldn’t. Then He walks us in like we belong — because now we do. If you feel too worn-out or too messed-up for joy this year, hear it again: the robe is a gift. Put it on.
days.prayer: Lord, thank You for dressing me in what I never could afford. I’ll wear it with joy. Amen.

days.title: He Sings Over You
days.verse: The Lord thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
body: Picture a mother rocking a baby late at night by the woodstove, humming some old hymn without even thinking about it. Not performing. Just singing, because she loves that child and the house is quiet.

That’s the picture Zephaniah paints, and it’s almost too good to be true. “He will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.” The God who is “mighty” — the One who saves — is also the One who sings over you.

We talk a lot about our joy in God. This verse turns it around: God has joy in you. He isn’t putting up with you. He isn’t tolerating you until you improve. He’s rejoicing. Whatever voice has been loudest in your head lately, sit still a minute and listen for a different one. Somebody’s singing over you.
days.prayer: Mighty God, quiet me with Your love, and let me hear You singing. Amen.

days.title: Send Portions
days.verse: Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the Lord is your strength.
body: The people had just heard God’s law read aloud, and they were weeping — convicted, ashamed of how far they’d drifted. And Nehemiah tells them: dry your eyes. Go eat. Drink something sweet. “This day is holy.” “The joy of the Lord is your strength.”
Tucked in the middle is a line that’s easy to miss: “send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared.”

That’s a mountain instinct if there ever was one. Somebody’s sick, somebody’s grieving, somebody’s had a baby — and here come the casserole dishes with masking-tape names on the bottom. Joy in these hills has always traveled by covered dish. God’s joy isn’t meant to stay at our table. It’s strength for us and supper for somebody else. Who around you has nothing prepared this Christmas? Make a plate. Joy grows when you give it away.
days.prayer: Lord, let Your joy be my strength, and show me whose table needs a portion. Amen.

days.title: Fear Not
days.verse: And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.
body: The shepherds were the night-shift crew — out in the cold, smelling of sheep, nobody’s idea of important people. And the first words they heard from heaven were “Fear not.”

That’s how God so often opens. To Abraham, to Joshua, to Joseph, to Mary, to the shepherds: fear not. Maybe because He knows the first thing we feel when heaven gets close is fear. We figure we’re in trouble.

But the news isn’t trouble. It’s “good tidings of great joy.” And it’s “to all people” — not just priests and kings, not just the respectable. Shepherds counted. That means you count. Whatever you’re afraid of this week — the bills, the test results, the holidays themselves — let the angel’s first words be the first ones you hear today. Fear not. The news is good, and it’s for you.
days.prayer: Lord, quiet my fear with Your good news. I’m one of the “all people.” Amen.

days.title: Coming Home Singing
days.verse: And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
body: Anybody who’s moved away from the mountains knows the feeling of driving home — the moment the hills start rising up on both sides of the road and something in your chest lets go. You’re not there yet, but you’re close.

Isaiah describes the greatest homecoming of all. “The ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads.” Picture a whole crowd walking home singing, joy sitting on their heads like a crown they can’t take off.

Then comes the best line: “sorrow and sighing shall flee away.” Sorrow doesn’t just fade. It runs. It can’t stand to be in the same room with what God is bringing. That’s where Advent points — not only to a manger, but to the day everything’s made right. As the week of joy closes, look on down the road. Home is closer than it looks.
days.prayer: Lord, bring me home singing, and let sorrow run. Amen.

days.title: So Loved
days.verse: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
body: It may be the best-known verse in the Bible. You’ve seen it on billboards along the interstate, painted on the side of a barn, held up at ballgames. It’s so familiar we slide right past it.

So slow down on two little words: “so loved.” Not loved, sort of. Not loved, on condition. So loved — loved this much, loved this way — that He gave. Love that only talks isn’t worth much in the mountains. Love here has always meant showing up: digging out a neighbor’s drive, sitting up with the sick, bringing what you’ve got. God’s love showed up. It gave the most precious thing it had, wrapped up in a baby.
Today we light the fourth candle, the candle of love. Look at all four burning together — hope, peace, joy, and now love. Love is what holds the other three up. And it starts with His.
days.prayer: Father, thank You for loving me enough to give. Teach me to love like that. Amen.

days.title: No Room
days.verse: And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
body: The longest night of the year falls right about now, and it’s fitting we read this verse in the dark: “there was no room for them in the inn.”

We’ve all known a no-room kind of place. The table where you weren’t welcome. The church that looked at you sideways. The family that closed ranks. Jesus knew it from His first night on earth. The Son of God came into the world He made and got sent out back with the animals.

But look what Mary did. She took what she had — swaddling cloths and a feed trough — and made it a place of love. A manger isn’t much. Neither was the barn behind Papaw’s house. But love can turn a stall into a sanctuary. Is there somebody who needs you to make room this week? A seat at your table doesn’t have to be fancy. It only has to be open.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I’ve got room for You. Help me make room for others too. Amen.

days.title: Unto You
days.verse: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord.
body: Read it slow and catch two words: “unto you.” The angel could have said a Saviour is born for the world, for the nation, for the religious folks up at the temple. All true. But he says it to a handful of shepherds in a cold field: unto you.
The gospel always gets personal. It’s one thing to believe Jesus came for people in general. It’s something else to believe He came for you — your history, your family, your ordinary Tuesday.

And look at the three names: Saviour, Christ, Lord. A Saviour rescues you. Christ means the Anointed One, the promised King. Lord means He’s in charge. You need all three. A Saviour who isn’t Lord is just a helper. A Lord who isn’t Saviour is just a boss. Jesus is both — and He came unto you.
days.prayer: Jesus — my Saviour, my Christ, my Lord — thank You for coming unto me. Amen.

days.title: Glory First
days.verse: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.
body: One angel was startling enough. Then “suddenly” the whole sky filled up — a multitude, more than anybody could count, like the stars over Spruce Knob on a clear winter night when there’s no town light for miles.

And what did they sing? Two things that belong together. “Glory to God in the highest” — that’s upward. “On earth peace, good will toward men” — that’s outward. When heaven gets its due, earth gets its peace.

We tend to flip it. We try to make peace on earth first, on our own steam, and fit God in when there’s time. It never holds for long. Peace runs downstream from glory. With everything rushing toward tomorrow, take a minute tonight — step out on the porch and look up — and give God the glory first. Then go be peace to somebody.
days.prayer: Glory to You, God, in the highest. Now make me peace on earth. Amen.

days.title: With Haste
days.verse: And they came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger.
body: The shepherds didn’t wait till morning. They didn’t wait till they’d cleaned up or found somebody to watch the sheep. They “came with haste.” And what did they find? Not a palace. Mary, Joseph, and a baby lying in a feed trough — exactly what they’d been told. God’s signs are usually that ordinary, and that sure.

Tonight we light the white candle in the center, the Christ candle. All Advent long we’ve been circling it: hope, peace, joy, love, each burning around an empty middle. Now the middle is lit. That’s Christmas. Everything we’ve been longing for finally has a center, and His name is Jesus.
Wherever you are tonight — a candlelight service, a quiet kitchen, a hospital break room, a long drive home — make haste to the manger. He’s right where they said He’d be.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, I’m coming with haste. Thank You for being right where You promised. Amen.

days.title: He Moved In
days.verse: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
body: Merry Christmas.

Luke tells the Christmas story with shepherds and angels. John tells it in one sentence bigger than the whole sky: “The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” The God who spoke the mountains into being became a baby who had to be fed and burped and rocked to sleep.

That word “dwelt” means “pitched his tent.” He didn’t visit. He moved in. He set up camp in the middle of our ordinary, muddy, beautiful world. So there’s no kitchen too small, no holler too far back, no heart too broken for God to dwell in. He’s already come closer than we ever could have climbed.
Look around your Christmas today — the wrapping paper, the people, the noise, maybe the quiet. He is among us, “full of grace and truth.” All five candles are burning.
days.prayer: Word made flesh, welcome home. Dwell in this house and in my heart. Amen.

days.title: Enough Light for the Next Stretch
days.verse: Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.
body: The day after Christmas can feel like a letdown. The paper’s in the burn barrel, the kids are cranky, the fridge is full of leftovers. But the story isn’t over. Somebody’s still on the road.
The wise men had come a long way, following a star, to find a King they’d never seen. They didn’t have the whole map. They had one light and enough faith to keep moving toward it.

That’s how a lot of faith works. God rarely shows you the whole road. He gives you enough light for the next stretch — like headlights on a foggy mountain road. You can only see a hundred feet ahead, but a hundred feet at a time will get you all the way home. Christmas isn’t a finish line. It’s a starting point. The light’s still shining. Keep following it.
days.prayer: Lord, give me enough light for the next stretch, and the faith to keep going. Amen.

days.title: Open the Treasure
days.verse: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy. And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshipped him: and when they had opened their treasures, they presented unto him gifts; gold, and frankincense, and myrrh.
body: When the wise men saw the star stop over the house, they “rejoiced with exceeding great joy.” Matthew piles the words up like he can’t find one big enough.

Then they came in, fell down, and worshipped. And then — only then — they opened their treasures. Gold, frankincense, and myrrh: gifts for a King, for God, and for One who would die. Notice the order: joy, then worship, then giving. Generosity flows out of worship, not guilt.

You may not have gold or spices. But everybody has a treasure chest of some kind. Time. A way with a fiddle or a quilting needle. A good ear for somebody who needs to talk. A kitchen that’s always open. Christmas is over on the calendar, but the King is still in the house. What’s in your chest you haven’t opened for Him yet?
days.prayer: King Jesus, I bow down. Here’s what I’ve got — it’s Yours. Amen.

days.title: Now I Can Rest
days.verse: Then took he him up in his arms, and blessed God, and said, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation.
body: Simeon was an old man who’d been promised he wouldn’t die till he saw the Messiah. Imagine how many years he walked into that temple, scanning faces, going home disappointed.

Then one day a young couple from the country walks in carrying a baby, and Simeon knows. He takes the child up in his arms — those old, spotted, shaking hands — and blesses God. “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace.” He’d seen it. That was enough.

Most of us have older folks in our lives who’ve been faithful a long, long time. Simeon is a reminder to honor them — to sit and listen to their stories while we can. And some of us are getting to be Simeon ourselves. Faithfulness never goes out of style. God keeps His promises right up to the last day, and the last day can be full of peace.
days.prayer: Lord, let me see Your salvation, and live and die at peace in it. Amen.

days.title: Widen the Circle
days.verse: Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.
body: Simeon keeps singing, and his song gets wider. This salvation is prepared “before the face of all people.” Jesus is “a light to lighten the Gentiles” — the outsiders, the folks nobody expected to be included — “and the glory of thy people Israel.”
That’s a big circle. It takes in insiders and outsiders, the church family and the folks who’ve never darkened a church door. The light isn’t a flashlight pointed at a chosen few. It’s a sunrise.

Mountain people know something about being outsiders. We’ve been the punchline plenty of times. So we, of all people, ought to be the ones who widen the circle — who make sure the newcomer, the stranger, the kid nobody claims gets pulled into the light. Who’s standing just outside yours? Christmas light was never meant to be kept in a jar.
days.prayer: Light of the world, widen my circle the way You widened Yours. Amen.

days.title: Anna Told Everybody
days.verse: And she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem.
body: Anna was eighty-four, a widow most of her life, and she all but lived at the temple — praying, fasting, waiting. When she saw the baby Jesus she did two things: she “gave thanks,” and she “spake of him” to everybody looking for redemption. She couldn’t keep it to herself.

Every community has an Anna. The church lady who’s prayed for every kid in the county by name. The widow who calls on your birthday every single year. Folks like that never make the news, but they hold whole towns together on their knees.

Anna shows us what to do after Christmas: give thanks, and tell somebody. Not a sermon. Just “Let me tell you what I’ve seen.” There are people all around you looking for something to set things right. You might be the one who tells them it’s here.
days.prayer: Lord, make me thankful like Anna, and give me the nerve to tell somebody. Amen.

days.title: Right on Time
days.verse: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.
body: On the last day of the year, it’s natural to look at the clock. Where did the time go? What did I do with it?

Paul says Jesus came “when the fulness of the time was come.” Not early, not late — right on God’s schedule. All those centuries of promises and waiting — the stump of Jesse, the little town of Bethlehem, the four hundred quiet years — were God’s clock ticking toward exactly the right moment.

And why did He come? “To redeem” — to buy back — “that we might receive the adoption of sons.” God didn’t come just to fix us. He came to bring us into the family. Adopted. Named. Given a place at the table. Whatever this year held, it wasn’t wasted in God’s hands. Tonight, as the year runs out, remember: you’re not just forgiven. You’re family.
days.prayer: Father, thank You for Your perfect timing, and for making me Your child. Amen.

days.title: All Things New
days.verse: Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
body: Happy New Year. Somewhere out there this morning, snow is lying across a field without a single track in it.
Everybody makes resolutions today — lose weight, save money, read more. Most won’t last to February. That’s no knock on anybody; it’s just hard to make yourself new.

Paul isn’t talking about resolutions. He says that if anyone is in Christ, “he is a new creature.” Not a cleaned-up version of the old one. New. “Old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” That’s where Advent was pointing all along. The baby in the manger grew up, went to the cross, and rose again so we could be made new from the inside out.
So walk into this year like a fresh field of snow. The old tracks are gone. Thank you for walking through Advent with us.
days.prayer: Lord, make me new — not just this year, but every morning. Amen.
